subject: Biotechnology
title: Fragrance and Flavor Engineering
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Fragrance and Flavor Engineering.

hook.text: Engineered yeast produces rose fragrance — the same molecule as from petals, brewed in a steel tank.

buildup.text: Terpene synthases convert simple sugars into geraniol, linalool, and nootkatone — the scents of rose, lavender, and grapefruit.

discovery.text: Evolva and Firmenich produce nootkatone in yeast — replacing extraction from 400 kg of grapefruit per kg of oil.

twist.text: Consumers struggle with the concept — naturally identical molecules from yeast challenge ideas about what is natural.

climax.text: Nootkatone also repels ticks and mosquitoes — the EPA approved it as a bio-based insect repellent.

punchline.text: Same scent, microbial source — fermentation brews nature's best aromas.

quiz.question: What are terpene synthases?
options: Chemicals used to extract fragrances from plants
Enzymes that convert simple sugars into fragrance and flavor molecules
Synthetic molecules that mimic natural scents

details.summary: Synthetic biology engineers yeast and bacteria to produce fragrance and flavor compounds like vanillin, nootkatone, and saffron molecules from sugar. These bio-identical molecules replace scarce or expensive natural extracts and environmentally destructive harvesting practices.
details.whyItMatters: Natural vanilla takes years to grow and costs hundreds of dollars per kilogram. Fermentation-produced vanillin is chemically identical, sustainably sourced, and reliably available.
takeaways: Engineered yeast produces vanilla, citrus, and saffron flavor compounds from sugar
Bio-identical molecules are chemically the same as natural plant extracts
Fermentation protects ecosystems from overharvesting rare flavor sources

faq.question: How does yeast produce vanillin through synthetic biology?
faq.answer: Genes from plants and bacteria encoding the vanillin biosynthesis pathway are inserted into baker's yeast. The yeast converts glucose through a series of engineered enzymatic steps into vanillin. Fermentation in bioreactors produces vanillin continuously at commercial scale.

faq.question: Is fermentation-produced vanillin considered natural or artificial?
faq.answer: Regulations vary by region. In some jurisdictions, fermentation-produced molecules from natural gene sequences qualify as natural flavoring. The EU classifies them differently from the US. The molecule itself is chemically identical regardless of production method.
